claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who leaves at second two takes away.)
claims.note: Results: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; Fig. 4 caption: female 'broadly similar to the male and child'; Abstract calls the inverse relation 'surprising' (so 'odd' is fair). Binning starts at red blood cells: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)'. 'Roughly' is the paper's word, and the paper itself names the fat/muscle gap as the one exception ('With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'), which the script says at line 9. At second two the viewer has heard only 'Sort the cells in your body by size', which asserts nothing false; the first card is keyed to the spoken word 'roughly' (index.tsx, at(0, "roughly")), so 'ROUGHLY THE SAME' cannot be misread early as 'cells are the same size'.

claims.claim: ROUGHLY THE SAME
claims.note: As claim 1: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass ... in each logarithmic cell-size class'.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred published sources to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: Received 22 Feb 2023, published online 18 Sep 2023, PNAS 120(39), 26 Sep 2023. 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'more than 1,500 published sources for 400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems ... giving 1,264 cell groups'. 'We compile data to estimate cell mass, size range, and cell count', so 'estimate' (not 'count') is right. Cells are then binned by mass into size classes (Fig. 3).

claims.claim: 1,500+ SOURCES
claims.note: '>1,500 published sources'.

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: Methods: bins begin 'at the lower bound of erythrocytes'; 'We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes (blood platelets and the smallest haploid gamete cells)'. Dataset S1 confirms platelets (9e-12 g) and spermatids/spermatozoa (2.8e-11 g) are the only smaller entries. 'It sorted' correctly excludes them.

claims.claim: RED BLOOD CELLS
claims.note: As claim 5.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; sizes run 'from the smallest red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers', 'seven orders of magnitude'. The paper's size is mass, so 'heavier' is right. Dataset S1: the six heaviest mean cell masses are all skeletal myocytes (sartorius 7.2e-4 g, upper bound 1.9e-3 g); the heaviest non-muscle cell (A-alpha sensory neuron) has mean 6.3e-5 g. 7.2e-4 / 4e-11 = 1.8e7; even mean fibre mass (21.5 kg / 1.19e8 = 1.8e-4 g) over a typical red cell (~9e-11 g) is about 2e6.
As claim 7: 'more than a million-fold larger'. A floor, correctly marked '>'.

claims.claim: Now put those cells into size classes, each class twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes), beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'.

claims.claim: ×2 EACH CLASS
claims.note: As claim 9.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Fig. 3: count per class regressed on mass gives 'a slope near -0.97'; 95% CI -1.09 to -0.87. Per doubling: 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47 to 0.55), so 'about half'. 'On average' is needed and present: Fig. 3 bins scatter round the line (e.g. the first class sits below the second, and classes near 1e-5 g fall well below the fit).

claims.claim: HALF AS MANY
claims.note: As claim 11.

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: 'A slope near -1 implies a roughly inverse relation between cell size and count, such that an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'.

claims.claim: THEY CANCEL OUT
claims.note: As claim 13 ('offset').

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; Abstract goes further ('contribute an equal fraction'). The exception follows in the next sentence.

claims.claim: ABOUT THE SAME
claims.note: As claim 15.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass'; 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'. 'One exception' is the paper's own framing. Fig. 4B (male) read off the figure: the gap floor is about 0.05 kg against a mean of about 1.7 kg per class, the only class more than two orders below the peak (7 kg).

claims.claim: ONE DIP
claims.note: As claim 17.

claims.claim: In women the dip is smaller, and in a ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: The paper says it of one modelled body: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'. That reference female is the 60 kg ICRP model, built by scaling the male: skeletal myocyte sizes are multiplied by 0.625 and adipocyte counts are scaled by tissue mass. The dip sits between the fat and muscle peaks, and the paper notes that 'body fat varies widely among subjects' and that adipocyte and myocyte sizes change with 'obesity, or muscle atrophy'. So 'In women' turns a comparison of two reference models into a claim about all women, which the paper does not make. The child half ('a ten-year-old', singular) is fine. Change: 'In a typical woman the dip is smaller, and in a typical ten-year-old it is fainter still' (this matches 'Take a typical man' at line 11).

claims.claim: SMALLER IN WOMEN
claims.note: Same over-generalisation as claim 19. Change to e.g. 'SMALLER IN A TYPICAL WOMAN' (or 'TYPICAL WOMAN: SMALLER'), to match the fixed line.

claims.claim: Take a typical man. His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count'; 0.002% = 1 in 50,000. Recomputed from Dataset S1 (reference male): 1.19e8 striated skeletal myocytes out of 7.12e12 nucleated cells (36.49e12 total minus 29.37e12 non-nucleated) = 1 in 59,900. 'Typical man' = the 70 kg ICRP reference male (20-50 y, 176 cm), which the paper calls 'representative'.

claims.claim: A TYPICAL MAN, sub "70 KG (154 LB)"
claims.note: 'Male, (70 kg, 176 cm in height and 20 to 50 y of age)'. 70 x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, so '154 LB' is right.
As claim 21; '<' matches '<0.002%'.

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120); SI Appendix and Dataset S1 via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/supplementaryFiles
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'. SI: 'slightly less than 22 kg of myocyte mass'. Dataset S1: 21.5 of 44.3 kg = 48.6%.

claims.claim: ABOUT HALF
claims.note: As claim 24.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120); SI Appendix and Dataset S1 via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/supplementaryFiles
claims.note: Fig. 1: '45 kg of cell biomass'; SI notes to Fig. 2: 'a total of ~44.3 kg of cell mass'; Dataset S1 sums to 44.27 kg (male).

claims.claim: 45 KG, sub "99 LB"
claims.note: 45 x 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, so '99 LB' is right.

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: cell biomass 'excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. SI: 'The remaining mass in the 70 kg male resides in extracellular content, including water (18-19 kg), protein (~3.7 kg), and minerals (~3.3 kg, most of which are bone minerals)', which sums to 25-26 kg; 44.3 + 25 is about 70. 'Between them' = extracellular, the paper's word. The gut microbiome (cells, but about 0.2 kg) is within the rounding.

claims.claim: NOT CELLS, sub "25 KG (55 LB)"
claims.note: ~25 kg noncellular (claim 28). 25 x 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, so '55 LB' is right; 99 + 55 = 154 lb is consistent with card 11.

claims.claim: BETWEEN THE CELLS
claims.note: 'extracellular water, protein, and minerals'.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight (10^15 g), but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value, respectively'. Evaluated 'in a "pristine" state, before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'; today 'the upper one-third of the biomass spectrum has been severely truncated', so the past tense and 'most' are both needed and present. The PNAS paper cites this as the same pattern ('bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales', ref. 44). The ocean classes are tenfold; the line does not claim otherwise.

claims.claim: THE OCEAN TOO
claims.note: As claim 31.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.note: Discussion, Origins: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'; Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. The paper offers candidates (random growth processes, mismatched growth and division rates) but stresses that 'many simple mechanisms are possible'. 'No accepted process ... yet' matches 'no universally recognized process'; 'nobody knows why' matches 'remain unresolved'.

claims.claim: NOBODY KNOWS WHY
claims.note: As claim 33 ('remain unresolved').

claims.claim: NOT YET EXPLAINED
claims.note: As claim 33 ('no universally recognized process').

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at every size.
claims.note: '≈36 trillion cells in the male', of which non-nucleated blood cells ≈29 trillion; skeletal fibres 1.19e8 (Dataset S1). 'Roughly the same weight at every size' restates 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class' (Conclusion), after the dip was stated at line 9.

claims.claim: ROUGHLY THE SAME
claims.note: As claims 1 and 36.

claims.claim: Axis "CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE" from 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g
claims.note: Size is cell mass in g, on log axes in Figs. 3-4. The binned range, 4e-11 to 2.7e-3 g, fits inside 1e-11 to 1e-2. The log scale is labelled.

claims.claim: Mark "RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g"
claims.note: 'beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)', 'the lower bound of erythrocytes'. 'FROM' correctly marks it as a lower bound.

claims.claim: Mark "FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g"
claims.note: 'biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10^-6 g)'. Dataset S1: white adipocytes of 2.8e-7 to 8.9e-7 g carry most fat-cell mass (biomass-weighted mean 5.3e-7 g). '~' is apt.

claims.claim: Mark "MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g"
claims.note: 'myocytes (near 10^-4 g)'. Dataset S1: mean skeletal fibre = 21.5 kg / 1.19e8 = 1.8e-4 g.

claims.claim: 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the last, starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.note: Methods: factor 2, 'beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'. The top edge, 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.7e-3 g, covers the heaviest fibres in Dataset S1 (sartorius upper bound 1.9e-3 g).

claims.claim: Bars "NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC": a straight falling staircase
claims.note: A schematic of the fitted power law (slope -0.97, about -1 per doubling). It is labelled SCHEMATIC, and the voice says 'on average'. The real bins in Fig. 3 scatter round the line (first class below the second; a shortfall near 1e-5 g), but a schematic of the fit, labelled as one, meets A6.

claims.claim: Bars "WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC": roughly level, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.note: Fig. 4A caption: biomass per class shows 'little systematic variation with log cell mass'; the gap between the adipocyte and myocyte peaks is the named exception. Fig. 4B male, read off the figure: classes outside the gap lie within about 1 order of magnitude of the 1.7 kg mean (lowest: about 0.2-0.3 kg, including the last class), while the gap floor is about 0.05 kg. On a log scale, 'roughly level plus one dip' is a fair schematic, and it is labelled SCHEMATIC. (This assumes the single row is the man, as in Fig. 3.)

claims.claim: Three stacked rows "MAN", "WOMAN", "CHILD, 10" titled "WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC": level bars, the dip shallower in each row down, drawn for only the first 25 of the 26 classes
claims.note: The shallower dip in each row follows the paper's text ('less prominent in the reference female ... even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'). Leaving off the 26th class is the problem. In Fig. 4B that class holds about 0.2 kg (man), about 0.05 kg (woman) and about 0.05 kg (child), against row means of about 1.7, 1.5 and 0.8 kg. For the woman and child it falls about as low as the dip floor (about 0.05 kg) itself. So the rows that compare the dip across bodies leave out the one other class as deep as the dip, and the dip looks like the only feature. The SOURCES block gives the steep fall as the reason for the cut, which makes this a curated visual (A6/A3). Also, the paper's female/child comparison is made on linear axes (Fig. 4B); on a log scale the dip floors read about equal in all three rows, so the difference is mainly in the peak heights. Change: draw all 26 classes in each row and let the last class drop as in Fig. 4B. Or, if the rows stay cut, say so on screen (e.g. 'LARGEST CLASS NOT SHOWN'). Either way, don't draw the woman's dip shallower than the man's beyond what the rows' own scale shows; drawing the rows on a linear scale, like Fig. 4B, is the simplest faithful option.

claims.claim: Grid of 250 × 200 dots captioned "50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · FEWER THAN 1 MUSCLE FIBRE", one dot ringed
claims.note: 250 x 200 = 50,000. '<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' means fewer than 1 fibre per 50,000; Dataset S1 gives 0.83 per 50,000. The ringed dot shows the upper bound, and the caption says 'fewer than 1', so the drawing does not overstate.

claims.claim: Bar "ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG", half filled, labelled "MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF"
claims.note: 'about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'; Dataset S1 21.5 / 44.3 kg = 48.6%, so a half fill drawn with '≈' is right.

claims.claim: Bar extends with "NOT CELLS · 25 KG", label "70 KG MAN", "WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS"; lengths drawn 45:25
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption '~25 kg' of extracellular water, protein and minerals; SI breakdown 18-19 + 3.7 + 3.3 kg; reference male 70 kg. Drawn in proportion, 45:25, as the numbers require.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis "SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE", level bars titled "BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC", the first two bars higher and the last two lower
claims.note: Axis, title and shape are right: 'Total estimated historic ocean biomass in each order of magnitude size class is approximately 1 Gt ... with exceptions at either extreme'; pristine = pre-1850, 'before industrial-scale fishing and whaling'. But Fig. 2 has three raised bins at the small end, not two: the bacteria-dominated classes read about 2.5, 2.5 and 1.9 Gt in the upper 200 m (about 6.8, 7.0 and 4.6 Gt over the full depth), against a plateau of about 1 Gt. At the large end, the last two classes, the mammal ones at about 0.12 and 0.06 Gt, are the low ones, so 'last two lower' holds. Change: raise the first three bars, not two. A further option, not required: the mid-size fish bump (about 0.01-1 g at full depth) is one the authors 'hesitate to draw a strong conclusion about', so leaving it out of a schematic is fine.
